paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves two linked optimization problems: the upper problem depends on the outcome of the lower one. This paper studies stochastic, unconstrained problems where the available tools provide only gradients. That setting matters because methods requiring second derivatives of the lower objective can involve expensive calculations.

The authors introduce Fully First-order Stochastic Approximation, or F2SA, and establish finite-time convergence guarantees. Reaching an epsilon-stationary solution takes epsilon to the powers of −7/2, −5/2, and −3/2 iterations when noise affects both objectives, only the upper objective, or neither objective, respectively. Each iteration uses a constant number of samples. Stationarity is the target of these guarantees; it does not assert a globally optimal solution.

Adding momentum-assisted gradient estimates improves the first two iteration bounds to epsilon to the powers of −5/2 and −2, while leaving the deterministic bound unchanged. The paper also reports better practical performance than existing second-order approaches in MNIST data-hypercleaning experiments. Together, these results give a gradient-only method both theoretical support and an application-level demonstration.
icml-2023-a-fully-first-order-method-for.tldr: F2SA solves stochastic bilevel problems using only gradients, with finite-time stationarity guarantees and improved bounds from momentum.

paragraphs: Generative flow networks learn to sample compositional objects according to a target distribution whose normalization need not be known. The paper addresses a restriction of the existing framework: its focus on discrete spaces. That restriction limits the kinds of variables and modeling problems the framework can directly describe.

The authors develop a generalized theory that includes discrete, continuous, and hybrid state spaces. A hybrid space can contain both discrete and continuous elements. Bringing these cases into one theory makes the extension more than a separate continuous variant: the existing discrete formulation is included within the broader framework.

The experiments serve two purposes. They illustrate important parts of the theory and why its assumptions matter, and they test whether observations from discrete GFlowNets carry over to continuous settings. The authors report such empirical transfer and strong results against non-GFlowNet baselines on several previously studied tasks. The contribution therefore combines a broader mathematical foundation with evidence that the extension can be useful for probabilistic inference and modeling.
icml-2023-a-theory-of-continuous-generat.tldr: A generalized GFlowNet theory covers discrete, continuous, and hybrid spaces, with experiments supporting its continuous-space applications.

paragraphs: Probabilistic programming lets users describe a Bayesian model while software handles inference. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is a powerful sampling method for these models, but some models remain difficult for it to handle directly. Users may consequently need to restructure their models through techniques such as reparameterization, reducing the convenience of automated inference.

This paper explores automatic marginalization as part of the HMC sampling process. Marginalization simplifies an inference problem by integrating out some variables instead of sampling every variable explicitly. The proposed approach works with a graphical model extracted from a probabilistic program, connecting the program's model structure to the simplification used during inference.

The authors report substantial sampling improvements on real-world hierarchical models. The practical significance is that model simplification can become part of the inference machinery rather than depending entirely on manual intervention. The stated result concerns improved sampling in these hierarchical models, supporting automatic marginalization as a useful way to make probabilistic programming more effective on models that challenge direct HMC.
icml-2023-automatically-marginalized-mcm.tldr: Automatically marginalizing variables in probabilistic programs substantially improves HMC sampling on real-world hierarchical models.

paragraphs: The bootstrap quantifies statistical uncertainty by generating resampled datasets and refitting models. In high-dimensional problems, repeatedly performing those fits can make uncertainty estimation expensive. This paper asks how little resampling can suffice when the number of dimensions is large relative to the number of observations.

Using a recent cheap-bootstrap perspective, the authors show that valid coverage can be attained with as few as one resample, even in settings where dimension grows closely with sample size. Coverage concerns whether an uncertainty interval contains its target at the intended rate. The result establishes that very limited resampling can support valid uncertainty statements in the high-dimensional regimes studied.

The paper also presents experiments that validate the theoretical results and compare the approach with other benchmarks. Its significance lies in reducing the computational burden associated with repeated resampling and refitting. The possibility of using just one resample supports bootstrap implementation for large-scale problems, while the claim remains about attainable coverage in the analyzed setting rather than a universal prescription for every bootstrap application.
icml-2023-bootstrap-in-high-dimension-wi.tldr: A cheap-bootstrap approach can achieve valid high-dimensional uncertainty coverage with as few as one resample.

paragraphs: Chip placement determines where circuit modules sit on a chip canvas. Reinforcement learning has shown promise for this task, but lengthy training and weak transfer to unfamiliar circuits can make it costly to use. ChiPFormer addresses both issues by learning from a fixed collection of existing placement designs.

The paper formulates placement as offline reinforcement learning and introduces a decision-transformer approach for learning a transferable placement policy. Its multi-task setting allows offline designs to contribute to learning across circuits. The resulting policy can then be fine-tuned for unseen circuits, making reuse of placement experience central to the approach.

Across experiments on 32 circuits, the authors report significantly better placement quality and a tenfold runtime reduction relative to recent state-of-the-art approaches. These evaluations include public benchmarks and realistic industrial tasks. They also report that effective fine-tuning reduces placement runtime from hours to minutes. The findings support offline policy learning as a way to improve both placement quality and the time needed to adapt to a new circuit.
icml-2023-chipformer-transferable-chip-p.tldr: ChiPFormer learns transferable chip-placement policies from offline designs, improving placement quality and reducing runtime in experiments across 32 circuits.

paragraphs: Block coordinate descent optimizes groups of variables in sequence. This paper studies its Gauss-Seidel form with proximal regularization, which discourages overly large changes during an update. The method is widely applicable to constrained, nonconvex optimization, and the paper establishes a worst-case bound on how many iterations it needs.

For smooth nonconvex objectives with block-wise constraints, the authors prove convergence to an epsilon-stationary point within O(1/epsilon) iterations. This describes progress toward stationarity rather than a guarantee of finding the global optimum. Under a mild condition, the same bound remains valid when individual update steps are solved inexactly, making the analysis relevant to approximate implementations.

The authors apply the result to Wasserstein CP-dictionary learning: finding elementary probability distributions that approximate a collection of multidimensional joint distributions. Their algorithm operates in the dual space and uses both entropic and proximal regularization of the primal problem. This application connects the general complexity result to a concrete distribution-learning problem, yielding an algorithm described as both efficient and provable.
icml-2023-complexity-of-block-coordinate.tldr: The paper proves an O(1/epsilon) stationarity bound for proximal block coordinate descent and applies it to Wasserstein dictionary learning.

paragraphs: A variational autoencoder uses an approximate distribution over latent variables to learn from data. This paper studies mixtures of such approximations, with each component represented by a separate encoder network. The central question is how these components cooperate when trained together to maximize the evidence lower bound, or ELBO.

Building on multiple and adaptive importance sampling, the authors examine joint adaptation of mixture components. Empirically, the ELBO does not decrease as more components are added across several VAE architectures on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10. They also find improved latent representations on image and single-cell datasets. The reported monotonic behavior is an experimental finding, not a stated universal guarantee.

An extensive ablation study compares and combines mixture VAEs with normalizing flows, hierarchical models, and VampPrior. Several mixture variants achieve state-of-the-art log-likelihood results for VAE architectures on MNIST and FashionMNIST. These findings motivate the authors' recommendation to treat mixture VAEs as a standard option for flexible variational approximation, with benefits extending beyond the training objective to learned representations.
icml-2023-cooperation-in-the-latent-spac.tldr: Jointly trained mixture encoders empirically improve VAE objectives and latent representations as more components are added.

paragraphs: Data valuation asks which training examples help or harm a model. Shapley-based approaches can provide useful answers, but training many models makes them computationally demanding. Data-OOB offers an alternative for bagging models by using out-of-bag estimates and reusing weak learners that have already been trained.

The reuse is central to its scalability. The authors report evaluating one million examples with 100 input dimensions in less than 2.25 hours on a single CPU processor. They also provide a theoretical interpretation: when comparing two data points, Data-OOB identifies the same important point as the infinitesimal jackknife influence function. This connects its valuation to an established influence-based comparison.

Experiments on 12 classification datasets, each containing thousands of examples, evaluate the usefulness of the resulting values. Data-OOB significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art valuation methods at detecting mislabeled examples and selecting helpful or harmful subsets. The contribution therefore combines lower computational demands with evidence that its values support practical data-quality decisions, within its stated bagging-model setting.
icml-2023-data-oob-out-of-bag-estimate-a.tldr: Data-OOB reuses bagging models to value training examples efficiently, with strong results for detecting mislabeled and helpful or harmful data.

paragraphs: DS-1000 evaluates whether code-generation systems can solve practical data-science problems. It contains one thousand problems across seven Python libraries, including NumPy and pandas. Drawing the tasks from StackOverflow gives the benchmark a basis in varied questions that arise during real programming work.

Evaluation combines running test cases with checking constraints on API use or keywords. This allows the benchmark to assess both what a solution does and whether it follows requirements about how to do it. Among the Codex-002 solutions accepted by this evaluation, only 1.8% are incorrect. That figure describes incorrect acceptances for those evaluated outputs, rather than every possible aspect of evaluation accuracy.

The authors also slightly modify source problems so that memorizing the original posted solutions is insufficient to answer them correctly. Codex-002, the best public system reported in the abstract, achieves 43.3% accuracy. Together, realistic tasks, multiple evaluation criteria, and changes that resist direct memorization make the benchmark a focused test of data-science coding ability with substantial room for improvement.
icml-2023-ds-1000-a-natural-and-reliable.tldr: DS-1000 tests data-science code generation on realistic, modified programming problems with execution checks and constraints on solution form.

paragraphs: Biological organisms use internal rhythms to anticipate regular environmental changes. This paper investigates whether similar behavior can emerge in deep reinforcement learning agents. The authors train agents on a foraging task in an environment with reliable periodic variation and systematically examine how their behavior develops during learning.

The learned rhythm is endogenous, meaning it is internally generated, and entrainable, meaning it can synchronize with an external signal. It also adapts when the environmental signal shifts in phase, without additional training. This shows that the agents' timing behavior can adjust after learning, rather than remaining fixed to the original timing of the environment.

The authors investigate the mechanism through bifurcation analysis and phase response curves. Their dynamical-systems analysis identifies a stable periodic orbit in artificial-neuron dynamics, with a phase response that supports optimal synchronization between the agent and its environment. The contribution connects observed rhythmic behavior to an internal dynamical mechanism, explaining how environmental regularity becomes represented in the agent's ongoing neural activity.
icml-2023-emergence-of-adaptive-circadia.tldr: Foraging agents develop internal rhythms that synchronize with periodic environments and adapt to timing shifts without retraining.

paragraphs: Graph coarsening produces a smaller graph while trying to preserve properties of the original. Real graphs often include information attached to each node, so retaining connectivity alone can leave out relevant context. This paper develops an optimization-based framework that uses both the graph structure and node features during reduction.

The method jointly learns the smaller graph matrix and its corresponding feature matrix. This makes the treatment of structure and features part of the same optimization problem. The authors also guarantee that the resulting graph is epsilon-similar to the original for epsilon between zero and one, excluding one. They describe this similarity guarantee as the first of its kind to their knowledge.

Experiments on real and synthetic benchmark datasets demonstrate the framework's effectiveness across graph clustering, node classification, stochastic block model identification, and graph summarization. These applications show why a coarsened graph should retain both relationships and associated information. The paper's main contribution is a general framework that combines this joint preservation goal with a formal similarity guarantee and evidence across several graph tasks.
icml-2023-featured-graph-coarsening-with.tldr: An optimization framework jointly coarsens graph structure and node features while guaranteeing similarity to the original graph.

paragraphs: Score-based generative models learn functions describing data distributions at different noise levels. These distributions are connected by the Fokker-Planck equation, which describes how a density evolves during diffusion. The paper asks whether the learned score functions respect the corresponding relationship across noise levels.

The authors derive a score version of the Fokker-Planck equation. It expresses a self-consistency property that the true scores satisfy. They observe that scores learned through denoising score matching can fail to satisfy this equation despite strong empirical performance. This identifies a mathematical relationship that the usual training objective does not reliably enforce.

The paper proves that satisfying the score equation improves likelihood and the degree of conservativity, a property concerning consistency with a gradient field. It then adds a regularization term to denoising score matching to encourage that consistency. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution ties an additional training constraint directly to the diffusion process underlying the model, giving the regularizer a theoretical motivation alongside empirical support.
icml-2023-fp-diffusion-improving-score-b.tldr: FP-Diffusion improves score-based models by regularizing their learned scores to satisfy the diffusion process's underlying consistency equation.

paragraphs: GeCoNeRF addresses learning a neural radiance field from only a few input images. With sparse observations, the method supplies additional guidance at viewpoints that were not photographed. It does this through a consistency constraint that uses the scene geometry predicted during rendering.

At an unobserved viewpoint, a rendered depth map guides the warping of the available images into that view. Those warped images become provisional training targets. The method compares features rather than requiring exact pixel reconstruction, encouraging semantic and structural agreement while allowing colors to change with viewpoint. That distinction matters for representing view-dependent radiance.

Warped targets can be erroneous, so the framework includes a method for filtering incorrect warped solutions. It also introduces training strategies intended to stabilize optimization. The authors report results competitive with state-of-the-art few-shot NeRF methods. The contribution is a way to turn sparse observations into geometry-aware supervision while accommodating both imperfect warps and legitimate changes in appearance across views.
icml-2023-geconerf-few-shot-neural-radia.tldr: GeCoNeRF uses depth-guided image warping and feature-level consistency to train competitive neural radiance fields from few views.

paragraphs: Complex tasks can benefit from planning at multiple levels: choosing an intermediate goal and then selecting actions that reach it. Learning both levels from demonstrations is challenging, particularly with high-dimensional inputs. This paper proposes a way to identify useful subgoals in expert trajectories and build a model for planning over them.

The subgoal-discovery stage uses reinforcement learning. Its rewards are linked to how predictable low-level actions become when the current state and proposed subgoal are known. This connects the usefulness of a subgoal to its ability to explain action choices. The identified subgoals are then modeled with a vector-quantized generative model for higher-level planning.

In experiments, the algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art methods on complex problems requiring decisions over long horizons. The authors also report that planning allows it to find trajectories better than those in its training set. The significance is that demonstrations supply material for learning a planning hierarchy, while the resulting planner can use that hierarchy to improve on the demonstrated trajectories.
icml-2023-hierarchical-imitation-learnin.tldr: The method learns subgoals from expert demonstrations and plans over them, enabling improved performance and trajectories better than its training examples.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection aims to recognize inputs that differ from the data a model is expected to handle. HEAT approaches this by estimating the density of familiar, in-distribution examples in the feature space of a pretrained backbone. It is a post-hoc method, applied using an already trained representation.

The model combines existing density estimators with a hybrid energy-based formulation. For example, a Gaussian mixture model can provide a prior density estimate that HEAT complements. The aim is an estimate that is both accurate and robust. A second contribution uses the energy-based framework to bring density estimation into a unified form and combine several energy terms.

The experiments support the usefulness of both contributions: complementing prior estimators and composing energy terms. The authors report state-of-the-art out-of-distribution detection results on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 and the large-scale ImageNet benchmark. These findings show that modeling the distribution of learned features can provide an effective basis for detection, with the hybrid formulation improving the use of existing density estimates.
icml-2023-hybrid-energy-based-model-in-t.tldr: HEAT combines density estimators and energy-based modeling in pretrained feature spaces to achieve strong out-of-distribution detection results.

paragraphs: Supervised learning usually begins with a chosen loss function, but that choice can be ad hoc. This paper studies learning the loss together with predicted probabilities while preserving properness, a decision-theoretic property under which Bayes' rule is optimal. Its focus is extending this idea to multiclass classification.

Earlier approaches learn an inverse canonical link for binary problems, using a monotonic map from a real-valued score to a probability. LegendreTron extends the construction to multiple dimensions, mapping scores into the projected probability simplex. It uses the monotonicity of gradients of convex functions to support this extension and jointly learns proper canonical losses and multiclass probabilities.

The authors evaluate the method on domains with as many as 1,000 classes. On every evaluated dataset with more than ten classes, it outperforms the natural multiclass baseline under a t-test at the reported 99% significance level. The results support the practical value of learning a statistically principled loss alongside the model in the tested multiclass settings.
icml-2023-legendretron-uprising-proper-m.tldr: LegendreTron jointly learns proper losses and multiclass probabilities using a multidimensional extension of monotonic link learning.

paragraphs: An embodied agent searching a home must predict where objects are despite seeing only part of a changing environment. This paper represents the scene as a graph, with rooms and objects as nodes and their relationships as edges. Predicting object locations becomes link prediction under both change and partial observability.

The proposed Scene Graph Memory stores the observations accumulated by the agent. A neural architecture called the Node Edge Predictor extracts information from that memory to support efficient search. The combination gives the predictor access to observation history while addressing the fact that the agent never knows the entire current graph.

The authors introduce the Dynamic House Simulator to evaluate the approach on diverse changing graphs that follow semantic patterns typical of homes. They show that the predictor can learn object locations across environments with different movement dynamics, outperforming baselines in accuracy and adaptation to new scenes. The results support using accumulated graph observations to guide prediction when object relationships change and direct observations remain incomplete.
icml-2023-modeling-dynamic-environments-.tldr: Scene Graph Memory and a neural link predictor help agents locate objects in changing, partially observed household environments.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering organizes graph nodes into a tree of nested groups. This paper presents two efficient algorithms evaluated against Dasgupta's cost function, which provides the objective for judging the resulting hierarchy. The goal is to obtain a good clustering tree while keeping computation close to the cost of processing the input graph.

For graphs with a clear cluster structure, the algorithms run in nearly linear time in the input size and return a constant-factor approximation to the objective. The approximation guarantee bounds the tree's cost relative to the optimum without asserting exact optimality. The clear-cluster-structure condition is part of the stated result, so the guarantee concerns that class of input graphs.

Experiments compare the proposed approach with the previous state of the art on synthetic and real-world datasets. The authors report comparable or better clustering trees with much lower runtime. This combines a theoretical quality-and-efficiency result for well-clustered graphs with empirical evidence that the computational savings can accompany competitive hierarchical clustering quality.
icml-2023-nearly-optimal-hierarchical-cl.tldr: Two algorithms achieve constant-factor hierarchical clustering approximations in nearly linear time for graphs with clear cluster structure.

paragraphs: Quantiles describe values below which specified fractions of a distribution fall. This paper studies estimating many such values under differential privacy, given independent, identically distributed samples. The target is the underlying distribution's quantile function, a task relevant to applications such as private data generation.

The first approach privately estimates quantiles of the observed sample and uses them to estimate population quantiles. The authors examine the statistical properties of an existing recursive private-quantile algorithm in this setting. This distinction between sample and population quantiles matters because the desired answer concerns the distribution that generated the data, beyond the particular sample collected.

The second approach uses density estimation to estimate the quantile function uniformly over an interval. The paper identifies a tradeoff between these strategies: when many quantiles are needed, estimating the density is preferable to estimating the quantile function separately at specified points. The finding makes the number of requested quantiles an important consideration when choosing a private statistical estimation method.
icml-2023-private-statistical-estimation.tldr: For estimating many quantiles under differential privacy, the paper finds advantages in estimating a density rather than individual quantile values.

paragraphs: In a reward-mixing Markov decision process, each episode begins with a random choice among M hidden reward models. The agent then interacts for H steps without directly observing that choice. The learning goal is a policy whose total reward is close to the best achievable in this setting.

The paper introduces EM² for arbitrary M of at least two, extending earlier upper-bound results for two contexts. Its episode bound scales as epsilon⁻² times SᵈAᵈ and a polynomial in H and reward-support size Z raised to d, where d is O(min(M,H)). Thus, the number of latent contexts and episode length influence the exponent in the sample requirement.

The authors also prove a lower bound of (SA) raised to Omega(square root of M), divided by epsilon squared. This supports the necessity of super-polynomial sample complexity in M in the general setting. Together, the bounds clarify both learnability with few hidden reward contexts and the difficulty of scaling to many contexts; the upper and lower bounds are not presented as identical.
icml-2023-reward-mixing-mdps-with-few-la.tldr: EM² learns near-optimal policies with hidden reward contexts, while a lower bound shows why many contexts can require sharply more samples.

paragraphs: Images can show the same meaningful content at different rotations or positions. In applications such as wafer defect inspection, plankton microscopy, and cryo-electron microscopy, these acquisition differences can be unrelated to the semantic distinctions of interest. This paper aims to learn representations that separate image content from its orientation.

The proposed IRL-INR method combines an implicit neural representation with a hypernetwork. This architecture is used to obtain semantic representations disentangled from image orientation, addressing rotation and translation variation through representation learning. The desired result is a description of image content that is useful even when the way that content is positioned changes.

The authors show effective disentanglement on images more complex than those considered in prior work. They also combine the representations with SCAN and report state-of-the-art unsupervised clustering results. That downstream result gives practical significance to the representation objective: separating orientation from semantics can produce features that work well for grouping images without labels in the evaluated settings.
icml-2023-rotation-and-translation-invar.tldr: IRL-INR separates semantic image representations from rotation and translation, supporting strong unsupervised clustering when combined with SCAN.

paragraphs: SinDDM explores training a denoising diffusion model on just one image. Instead of drawing its training statistics from a large image collection, it learns the internal statistics of that single example. A multiscale diffusion process lets the model work with the image at different levels of detail.

The reverse diffusion process uses a lightweight, fully convolutional denoiser conditioned on both noise level and scale. Generation proceeds from coarse structure toward finer detail. The architecture permits output samples with arbitrary dimensions, making the learned image statistics usable beyond the original image's dimensions.

The authors illustrate diverse, high-quality samples and applications including style transfer and harmonization. They also show that external supervision can guide the model, demonstrating text-guided generation with a pretrained CLIP model. This distinguishes learning from one image from the separate use of a pretrained guidance model. The contribution is a diffusion framework that learns from minimal image-specific training data while supporting several forms of generation and editing.
icml-2023-sinddm-a-single-image-denoisin.tldr: SinDDM learns a multiscale diffusion model from one image to generate varied outputs and support editing and externally guided generation.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations are often expected to help downstream learning, but the paper notes that supporting understanding remains limited. It studies their interaction with sparse task-specific predictors: predictors that use only a subset of the available representation. The authors provide evidence that this combination improves generalization.

In multi-task learning, the paper proves an identifiability result giving conditions under which maximally sparse predictors yield disentangled representations. The conditions are central: the result does not say that sparsity always produces disentanglement. Motivated by this connection, the authors formulate a practical learning approach as a bilevel optimization problem that promotes sparsity.

They also develop a meta-learning version using group Lasso multiclass support vector machine predictors and derive a tractable dual formulation. It achieves competitive results on standard few-shot classification benchmarks while each task uses only a fraction of the learned representation. The findings connect a theoretical route to disentanglement with a practical method for learning shared features that individual tasks can use selectively.
icml-2023-synergies-between-disentanglem.tldr: Sparse task-specific predictors can support disentangled representations under stated conditions and yield competitive few-shot learning performance.

paragraphs: Data augmentation improves vision models by introducing transformed training examples, but its benefits can require long training schedules. The paper highlights this cost even for familiar augmentation methods. Tied-Augment aims to make augmentation effective across more training settings, including short runs and fine-tuning.

The framework adds a simple term to the training loss that controls how similar representations are under distortions. This acts on the relationship between learned representations of transformed inputs, supplementing the augmentation process itself. The approach is general enough to improve methods from augmentation, optimization, and semi-supervised learning, including RandAugment, mixup, SAM, and FixMatch.

The authors report that Tied-RandAugment can outperform RandAugment by 2.0% on ImageNet. They also show that augmentation can improve generalization with only a few training epochs and during fine-tuning when used with Tied-Augment. These findings matter because they broaden the situations in which augmentation is useful, linking its effectiveness to explicit control over the representations produced from distorted examples.
icml-2023-tied-augment-controlling-repre.tldr: Tied-Augment controls representation similarity under distortions to improve augmentation, including during short training runs and fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Detecting that data have changed does not by itself explain what changed. Such distribution shifts may signal a different operating environment or reduce a model's accuracy. This paper aims to help human operators understand shifts by describing transformations from the original distribution to the shifted one.

The method constructs interpretable transportation maps through a relaxation of optimal transport. Candidate maps are restricted to an interpretable family, making understandability part of the problem formulation. The resulting explanation describes how the original distribution can be transformed toward the new one, giving more information than a simple indication that a shift exists.

The authors demonstrate the approach on real-world tabular, text, and image examples. Visual inspection and their PercentExplained metric indicate a better balance between explanatory detail and interpretability than baseline explanations. The stated aim is to aid manual mitigation by making shifts easier to examine. The contribution is therefore an explanation method with supporting evaluations, rather than a claim that producing an explanation automatically fixes downstream performance.
icml-2023-towards-explaining-distributio.tldr: Interpretable transport maps explain distribution shifts by describing transformations from the original data distribution to the changed one.
